How should China build public trust in autonomous driving?

A white paper on transparency, evidence, and governance — the three things that turn a capable machine into a trusted one.

00Executive summary

The binding constraint has moved. It is no longer capability. It is trust.

The professionals interviewed for this report are nearly unanimous that the core technology is now, in one product manager's words, "commercially usable." Yet deployment stays cautious, public understanding stays thin, and adoption trails what the engineering alone would permit.

Trust is not manufactured by safety, and it is not manufactured by claims. It is built by a chain: transparency creates trust, evidence sustains it, and governance protects it. Technology creates capability, policy creates accountability, and education creates trust — and none of the three substitutes for the others.

The report's central contribution is the TRUST Framework for Autonomous Driving Governance, built on five reinforcing pillars, and the five recommendations that flow from it — anchored by a signature proposal, a two-tier autonomy label. China does not begin this work from behind: it begins from a decisive deploy-first posture, a disciplined whitelist-and-rings rollout, and unusually high public trust in its own institutions.

01Reframing the question

"Is it safe?" is the wrong question.

Safety is not a switch a vehicle flips on or off. It is a probabilistic, conditional claim about how a vast system behaves across circumstances so wide that most of them are rare. Ask an honest engineer whether a car "is safe," and the honest answer is another question: safe where, safe when, and safe compared to what?

What institutions, evidence, and communication allow society to determine whether autonomous driving is safe enough?
The question this report is built to answer

The move matters because it turns an unanswerable technical question into a chain of answerable institutional ones. "Safe enough" implies a threshold. A threshold implies someone who decides. A decision implies evidence; evidence implies disclosure; disclosure implies a public able to read it; and reading it implies someone who can be held to account. Each link is a policy lever, and the rest of this report pulls on them one by one.

Beneath the argument sits a simple equation. Technology creates capability — what a system can do. Policy creates accountability — who is answerable when it acts. Education creates trust — whether the public can judge the first two. Enthusiasm with no real capability produces the most dangerous outcome of all: misplaced trust. The three must climb together, or whatever is built on one alone will not hold weight.

02The current landscape

Deploy first, regulate later — by design, not by drift.

China's approach fits one phrase that recurred across nearly every interview: 先跑先试. Rather than wait for a finished legal code, regulators permit bounded real-world deployment and let the rules converge on what the evidence reveals. The posture runs on three mechanisms.

Mechanism 1

Whitelist

Nothing is permitted by default. A company must prove a capability before its permissions widen — the mirror image of a default-allow posture.

Mechanism 2

Ring rollout

Operators earn scope geographically: accumulate safe mileage in outer zones, then apply to move inward toward the dense core.

Mechanism 3

Staged ODD

Closed road → open road with a safety driver → driverless, each stage gated by its own bar; incidents graded P0/P1/P2.

The risk

Shock sensitivity

One high-profile episode — the Wuhan incident — set off a wave of tightening. Governance is adaptive, but its adaptations can arrive all at once.

Nothing is allowed by default. You must prove capability before scope opens.
Business & operations lead

Two brains, two bets

The industry is split between a sensor-and-map-heavy path — redundant LiDAR, radar, cameras, HD maps — and a data-driven path with minimal sensors and maximum learned intelligence. A commercialization strategist gave the report its most memorable image:

Very strong eyes, a five-year-old's brain — versus limited senses, an adult expert driver's brain. Both still carry safety and risk.
Commercialization strategist

And the capability itself is real, but bounded. Consumer L2 assistance and true L4 autonomy are different products with different purposes. As one deployment specialist put it, L2 "only needs 70 to 80 points; its goal is just to sell cars, not to solve the A-to-B problem." Treat the two as neighboring points on one line — in marketing or in regulation — and you manufacture exactly the confusion this report exists to fight.

03Key challenges

The trust deficit is not one problem. It is five, braided together.

Why, if the technology is already "commercially usable," does trust lag so far behind? Weak evidence makes disclosure hollow. Opacity makes accountability impossible. Confusion about capability makes every other problem worse. None can be solved alone.

→ Safety Validation

The evidence problem

Proving a system safe is a statistical ordeal — the long tail is precisely the events that happen least often. A deployment specialist's ceiling: of 100 hard cases, a system may solve 98 and fail the last two — and a human would fail those two as well. Permanent, not transitional.

→ Transparency

The transparency problem

Incident data is not systematically public, and modern deep-learning models are not mathematically traceable the way rule-based ones were. An algorithm developer named interpretability the field's single biggest bottleneck: "nobody ever tells you what 100 looks like."

→ Understanding

The communication problem

The public learns capability through marketing, which is built to blur the distinctions that matter. With no standardized vocabulary, no consumer — or regulator — can compare two products side by side. A latent public-safety problem in its own right.

→ Responsibility

The accountability problem

Who is responsible swings sharply across L2, L3, and L4 — and the public rarely knows which product it is sitting in. In L2 the human is still the legal driver; in L4 the black-box problem makes fault hard to establish even when the will to assign it is there.

People accept human error as fate, but cannot accept a machine erring — and so demand something close to perfection before they will extend any trust at all.
Operations lead — on the asymmetry at the centre of the trust gap

A fifth challenge cuts across all the others, because it is about people, not machines: automation complacency (a system good enough to trust is easy to stop watching); the exposure gap (trust cannot grow from an experience almost no one has had); friction that is not about safety (the top complaint is fixed pickup points, not crashes); and induced behavior — a perception engineer described pedestrians who, having learned that autonomous vehicles yield reliably, now step out on purpose. The technology reshapes the very environment it then has to survive in.

04Comparative analysis

Four countries, four characteristic bets.

Other countries appear here as case studies, not a scoreboard. Each has placed a bet, and each bet carries both a lesson and a limit for China. The transferable ideas are the mechanisms, pried loose from the institutions that produced them.

United States

Disclosure

The bet: incident reporting, public disengagement data, and a dense layer of media, insurers, and advocates who translate it.

The limit: that interpreter ecosystem does not exist in the same form in China — raw numbers few could use.

Germany

Law first

The bet: legislated an L3 framework early, aligned to international type-approval. Responsibility defined before deployment.

The limit: a type-approval culture moves deliberately — in tension with deploy-first speed.

Singapore

Standards + sandbox

The bet: national technical standards paired with well-defined testbeds and phased expansion, designed together.

The limit: a city-state does not generalize to China's scale — though the sandbox mechanism travels.

Japan

Caution

The bet: advancing L3 and limited L4 through careful legal amendment, with public confidence the explicit priority.

The limit: deliberate trust-building comes, again, at the cost of speed.

In the US, safety reports are public, and media, NGOs, and insurers serve as intermediaries.
Commercialization strategist — drawing the contrast with China

What does not transfer is the assumption of a Western-style intermediary layer. Because China's trust runs through the state, disclosure should be designed to flow first to regulators and qualified third parties, with a deliberate, staged path toward public reporting — not a sudden switch to full openness.

05The TRUST framework

Five pillars that hold each other up.

Every partial fix is undone by the gaps around it. Disclosure without validated data discloses noise. Validation without disclosure convinces no one. Accountability without interpretability cannot be enforced. The framework couples five pillars designed to hold each other up — a cycle, not a list.

T

Transparency

Capabilities, ODDs, limitations, and safety data through standardized reporting, not marketing language. Converts private engineering knowledge into public knowledge.

R

Responsibility

Legal responsibility across L2/L3/L4 defined in advance, in terms a consumer can understand. What makes transparency bite.

U

Understanding

Public technological literacy raised through experiential tools, not lectures. What gives transparency an audience. Trust the Machine is one such tool.

S

Safety Validation

Standardized testing, simulation benchmarks, third-party audits, post-deployment monitoring. What produces the evidence transparency discloses.

T

Trustworthy Governance

Adaptive regulation that evolves with the technology while holding a stable safety floor — balancing innovation against accountability and public confidence. The pillar that keeps the other four current as the technology moves beneath them.

06Recommendations

Five moves, one per pillar.

Each is specified by who acts, what benefits follow, and what it costs. The reforms are sequenced: the disclosure and shared-vocabulary reforms (R1 and R3) come first, because a common language and comparable data are what every later reform stands on.

R1

Standardized disclosure, anchored by a two-tier autonomy label Transparency

Why
Closes three gaps at once: incompatible marketing vocabularies, the invisible ODD, and missing disengagement/incident data.
Who
The regulator (MIIT) sets a mandatory label format and machine-readable ODD schema; a certification body verifies; a qualified third party aggregates.
Tension
A fully public raw-data label cuts against the managed model — resolved by two tiers: full data for regulators, a legible subset for consumers.
R2

Clear liability by level, made enforceable by reconstructable evidence Responsibility

Why
Accountability is most ambiguous exactly where products differ most — and cannot be enforced if the decision cannot be reconstructed.
Who
Legislators and courts define liability by level, building on pilots like Shenzhen's; the regulator mandates a standardized event data recorder.
Cost
Rules set too early may not fit future tech; event recording brings data-volume, privacy, and cost burdens.
R3

A national public-understanding program on a shared vocabulary Understanding

Why
Transparency is worthless without an audience able to read it, and the exposure gap means most people have no direct experience to reason from.
Who
Government and educators with industry support, drawing on experiential tools including Trust the Machine; a standards body fixes the terminology.
Cost
If industry-led, it risks reading as promotion rather than education.
R4

Independent validation, before and after deployment Safety Validation

Why
Self-attestation cannot carry trust once stakes climb; safety is continuous — systems change with every update, and the long tail shows only in operation.
Who
Accredited certifiers and qualified third parties under regulator oversight, with operators supplying data and their existing P0/P1/P2 monitoring.
Cost
Expense, potential slowdown, a checkbox-culture risk, and surveillance concerns from continuous monitoring.
R5

Adaptive regulation on a stable safety floor, learned through sandboxes Governance

Why
Formal sandboxes give the deploy-first instinct a controlled, evidence-generating structure — and lower the chance one incident forces a blunt, system-wide reaction.
Who
National and municipal regulators, extending the existing ring model into formal sandboxes and coordinating adaptive rules across departments.
Cost
Fragmentation if every city runs an incompatible sandbox; adaptivity that can slide into unpredictability if undisciplined.
07Future outlook

The road ahead is less straight than public debate assumes.

L4 to L5 is not a smooth upgrade.

L5 — operation in all conditions — may not be reachable by scaling today's four-wheeled robotaxi at all. Policy should treat L4-within-defined-ODDs as the operative regime, and resist framing L5 as imminent.

Geography will shape deployment more than raw capability.

Commercial viability concentrates in dense urban demand; rural service is navigable but not viable; inter-city runs into high-speed rail and cross-jurisdiction approval. The Greater Bay Area is a favorable exception, not a template.

The floor-versus-ceiling tension will not resolve soon.

Sensor-heavy routes offer a high safety floor and lower ceiling; data-driven routes the reverse. Governments prize the floor; the public wants both at once. Governance should hold the floor while leaving room for the ceiling to rise.

China does not have to choose abruptly.

The framework's staged path — regulator-tier data first, qualified third parties next, graduated public reporting over time — lets trust migrate from resting on an institution to resting on visible evidence, at a pace the institution can control.

08Conclusion

Getting the vehicles right is engineering. Getting the decision right is policy.

Autonomous driving in China is no longer held back mainly by what the technology can do. It is held back by whether society can tell how safe it is, hold someone answerable when it fails, and understand it well enough to trust it for the right reasons. Those are not engineering problems. They are problems of transparency, evidence, and governance.

The right question was never whether autonomous driving is safe. It is whether we are building the evidence, the accountability, and the shared understanding that let a society decide — and keep deciding — whether it is safe enough.

This report is a proposal that China take that second task as seriously as it is already taking the first.

Method & appendices

A · Method

Nine semi-structured interviews conducted in 2025–2026 with professionals across operations, deployment and data, perception and planning engineering, product management, test operations, and commercialization strategy. Cited by role to protect candor. Supported by desk research on the mid-2026 landscape, organized with a knowledge graph across the interview corpus.

B · The framework at a glance

Five pillars — Transparency, Responsibility, Understanding, Safety Validation, Trustworthy Governance — a reinforcement cycle, and a mapping from each of the five challenges of Section 3 to its pillar and recommendation.

C · Signature visuals

Full-size versions of the Trust Flywheel, the Whitelist Ring Map, the Trust Gap chart, the TRUST Framework diagram, and the two-tier Autonomy Label (Figures 1–5 above).

D · Glossary

ODD (Operational Design Domain); SAE levels L2–L5; disengagement; corner case and long tail; 先跑先试 (deploy-first, regulate-later); whitelist and ring-based rollout; P0/P1/P2 incident grading; safety floor versus ceiling.

A public-interest education project. The crashes and testimonies in the companion experience are dramatized; the numbers and the insights behind them are not. This document argues for the rules, evidence, and communication China needs — not the ones it already has.
